title: Shankara and the man on the path
hook: a famous scholar tells a man to get out of his way, and the man answers with a question about the Self
carry: jnana is knowing the one self in everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last kirtan song: the aarti, a flame offered to the light behind every light. Everything shines by his light. Now the singing goes quiet, and a book opens.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `EVERYTHING SHINES BY HIS LIGHT.` · `NOW, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Kashi, early morning. A young teacher, already famous for his learning, is walking up from his bath in the Ganga with his students. Coming toward him down the narrow lane is a man of the lowest caste, the kind the society of the day called untouchable, with four dogs at his heels. The teacher does what custom told him to do. Move aside, he says. Get out of the way. The man doesn't move. He asks a question.
screen: `KASHI, AFTER THE MORNING BATH.` → `'MOVE ASIDE.'` → `THE MAN ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The teacher, tradition says, was Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita, non-duality. And the man's question, as the story is told: what do you want moved away? This body made of food, from that body made of food? Or awareness from awareness? Is the sun any different, reflected in the Ganga or in a puddle in a poor man's lane? Shankara stops. He has taught exactly this: that the one Self, Brahman, is the same in every being. Now a man in the street has shown him that he knew it only as an idea. He bows, and a short poem credited to him says: whoever sees this way, whether outcaste or high-born, is my teacher. Many tellings add that the man was Shiva himself, and the four dogs the four Vedas. That's jnana. Not knowing about, the way you can know the capital of a country you've never seen. Knowing directly, the way you know you're awake. The book we open this week, the Vivekachudamani, the crest-jewel of discernment, also credited to Shankara, warns about this right away. A flood of words and skill in explaining scripture give the learned a kind of enjoyment, it says, but they don't set anyone free. Without realizing the oneness of the Self, there is no freedom. So on this teaching, you can't tell real jnana by what someone can recite. You can tell it by how they treat the person in the lane.
screen: `'BODY FROM BODY, OR SELF FROM SELF?'` · `SHANKARA BOWS.` · `JNANA: KNOWING, NOT KNOWING ABOUT.` · `CLEVER TALK DOESN'T FREE.` · then, large: `ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll pass today without really seeing: the one who cleans, the driver, the auntie stacking chairs after the program. For a few breaths, set down the labels, the job, the clothes, the place in line, and rest on the plain fact that they're aware, just as you are. That shared awareness is what Shankara's teaching calls the one Self. If you pray, bow inwardly to the Lord in them, as Shankara bowed in the lane; if not, simply notice how the labels loosen.
Jnana. Knowing, the direct kind, not knowing about. In Shankara's story it's the knowing that sees one Self in the man in the lane, which no amount of clever talk can stand in for.
Your line: jnana is knowing the one self in everyone. Not borrowed, but seen. See you tomorrow.

Vivekachudamani.meaning: the crest-jewel of discernment, a teaching poem credited to Shankara

Shankara.meaning: the teacher of Advaita, credited with this book

Advaita.meaning: non-duality: the teaching that the Self is one

Viveka.meaning: discernment: telling the lasting from the passing

Kashi.meaning: Varanasi, the holy city on the Ganga

Manisha Panchakam.meaning: five verses credited to Shankara, told with this story
